posts.text:
having worked at facebook for many years, i witnessed exactly how social media gradually lost its value of being social

facebook used to be about updates from friends you care about. but everyone only has so many good friends, and the friends only have so many updates worth posting

how do you grow from there? you either 
1. add content that people don’t really care about
2. add content that people do care about, but aren’t from their friends

1 is obviously a bad strategy. number 2 however is good for engagement and infinitely scalable

so the engagement-maxxing began, and it overshadowed content from friends. once the growth game starts and everyone’s performance review and bonus is tied to it, there’s no turning back

if we went back to 2004, how would we solve this? 

i think we should have stopped trying to grow facebook. let it be a stable network of just your friends. optimize for weekly activity instead of time spent. checking in on your friends once a week is okay - it’s a sick world if people check in on their friends every 5 minutes. the growth only needs to be at the same pace as the world population, nothing more

grow instagram to be the interest based platform instead. do all the engagement-maxxing there. keep a clear separation of facebook’s mission from instagram

the lack of clarity in strategy is what destroyed the real friendship based social platform we used to have, and we should have kept it alive

what do you think?

posts.text:
there is a mass misconception that $MSFT is cancelling Claude Code licenses because of the bill

it’s not the bill

they are migrating employees using claude code to copilot, and guess what LLMs copilot need to call, and how the tokens get charged? 

microsoft does not own a frontier model, which means all the tokens they use have to come from another provider, charged at API pricing (they do get a volume discount whether through claude code enterprise plan or API)

maybe some of their employees will shift to gpt as a result of not being locked in to claude and that’s a bit cheaper, but in the grand scheme of things, the difference doesn’t really make a dent in microsoft’s pocket to justify a walk-back like this

what’s happening then? 

it’s politics. having their own employees using claude code instead of copilot creates bad internal optics as well as external brand image

people in charge of copilot must have been screaming everyday “copilot can do the same things”, “we need to dogfood our own company’s product”, “it’s better to not lock in to a single vendor” - some of these arguments are legit, and they just won

that’s how they cancelled claude code. not because of the bill which will continue to come, but because there are powerful people with strong incentive to drive the change

this just became a fascinating thread about models and harnesses. lots of good discussions and even openai chimed in - thanks everyone who offered thoughts!

let me recap the essence of the key arguments here:

"it's in the model companies' business interest to do so"
i have no doubt about this. models are becoming commodity, they need vertical integration, owning the customer relationship etc - these are valid business strategies. my argument is not about why they would do it, but whether it's a good thing for the world

"the harness is part of how they train the model"
yes, but i have a few problems with this:
1. training the model to work with a specific harness makes the model overfit to it. imagine nvidia starts making GPUs only work for their own models
2. instead, they can use a wide variety of 3p harnesses in training, so the models can generalize well to how the world really wants to use them
3. even if they want to use their own harness for training the model, they can publish the harness as a spec or research paper, and let the ecosystem innovate on top of it. but both anthropic and openai are heavily marketing the harness as the revenue generator now

"the harness is how they collect telemetry to improve the model"
this is totally valid. i still think this can potentially be done via the model API - if your harness follows certain conventions when calling the API and allow data collection, you get a 50% discount on API pricing - this is much more scalable as an ecosystem than relying on getting every user to use the model company's 1p harnesses. they'll get more diverse training data as well

all that said, i should add that i appreciate how OpenAI has allowed 3p harnesses to integrate with the codex subscription and kept codex cli open source since the beginning - this is a lot more friendly to the developer ecosystem than what some other model company is doing, and i think over time this earns OpenAI more trust and makes them a more reliable brand for everyone to count on as a platform

quote.text:
The vibes in SF feel pretty frenetic right now. The divide in outcomes is the worst I've ever seen.

Over the last 5yrs, a group of ~10k people - employees at Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, Nvidia, Meta TBD, founders - have hit retirement wealth of well above $20M (back of the envelope AI estimation).

Everyone outside that group feels like they can work their well-paying (but <$500k) job for their whole life and never get there.

Worse yet, layoffs are in full swing. Many software engineers feel like their life's skill is no longer useful. The day to day role of most jobs has changed overnight with AI.

As a result,
1. The corporate ladder looks like the wrong building to climb.
Everyone's trying to align with a new set of career "paths": should I be a founder? Is it too late to join Anthropic / OpenAI? should I get into AI? what company stock will 10x next? People are demanding higher salaries and switching jobs more and more.

2. There’s a deep malaise about work (and its future).
Why even work at all for “peanuts”? Will my job even exist in a few years? Many feel helpless. You hear the “permanent underclass” conversation a lot, esp from young people. It's hard to focus on doing good work when you think "man, if I joined Anthropic 2yrs ago, I could retire"

3. The mid to late middle managers feel paralyzed.
Many have families and don't feel like they have the energy or network to just "start a company". They don't particularly have any AI skills. They see the writing on the wall: middle management is being hollowed out in many companies.

4. The rich aren’t particularly happy either.
No one is shedding tears for them (and rightfully so). But those who have "made it" experience a profound lack of purpose too. Some have gone from <$150k to >$50M in a few years with no ramp. It flips your life plans upside down. For some, comparison is the thief of joy. For some, they escape to NYC to "live life". For others still, they start companies "just cuz", often to win status points. They never imagined that by age 30, they'd be set. I once asked a post-economic founder friend why they didn't just sell the co and they said "and do what? right now, everyone wants to talk to me. if i sell, I will only have money."

I understand that many reading this scoff at the champagne problems of the valley. Society is warped in this tech bubble. What is often well-off anywhere else in the world is bang average here.

Unlike many other places, tenure, intelligence and hard work can be loosely correlated with outcomes in the Bay. Living through a societally transformative gold rush in that environment can be paralyzing. "Am I in the right place? Should I move? Is there time still left? Am I gonna make it?" It psychologically torments many who have moved here in search of "success".

Ironically, a frequent side effect of this torment is to spin up the very products making everyone rich in hopes that you too can vibecode your path to economic enlightenment.

even if you don't maintain npm packages, this still helps

if you set the same minimum age policy i shared above, and only use pnpm to install npm packages, you will get the same guardrail that prevents you from accidentally getting a malicious package version

posts.creator: kunchenguid
posts.text:
pnpm v11 also made dependency build scripts explicit

this matters because when installing a dependency they can run build scripts which executes arbitrary code

so i explicitly allowlist what can execute:

```
onlyBuiltDependencies:
  - esbuild
allowBuilds:
  esbuild: true
```

posts.creator: kunchenguid
posts.text:
the obvious complication: i push updates to my own packages very often

if i released something myself, i usually want to install it immediately

so i need exceptions, and it's easily doable:

```
minimumReleaseAgeExclude:
  - my-own-package
```

posts.creator: kunchenguid
posts.text:
so i switched to using pnpm

still using the npm registry but pnpm helps enforce what packages i use

with pnpm, i just needed to set this config:

```
minimumReleaseAge: 10080
minimumReleaseAgeStrict: true
```

(`10080` is 7 days in minutes)

quote.text:
Amazing thread (thx for ping!) My response is a little long but the question of whether to (dis)allow internet is a meaningful one, so I'll do my best to recap my thought process:

To give some context, 2 core tenets of how I wanted to execute on this idea were to (a) standardize and (b) scale this setting. A lot of past case studies on 0-to-1 repo gen. (e.g. Anthropic, Cursor, METR) were really exciting, but they experimented on a handful of repo's w/ inconsistent settings. I care a lot about statistical power; that's a big reason why SWE-bench is popular imo

Therefore, a key question around standardizing is - yes or no internet? Very early on, i was actually very in favor of it for the very reasons @kunchenguid mentioned. Humans use the internet!

But 2 things happened:

(1) models cheat a crazy amount.

You tell it don't look at the source code, it looks at forks on GitHub. You say not that either - it looks at the dependency/tool management indexes (cargo, go.mod, pypi, homebrew). You block that, it finds a version on sourceforge. And then stackoverflow. The cat and mouse game is endless. It's worsened by the fact that each repo has its own form of "leakage" (the surface form area of potential cheating sources gets larger with more popular repos). We document this thoroughly in the appendix.

(2) From a more ideological standpoint, my attitude also shifted towards the position that internet access is helpful, but arguably not necessary. Many of these codebases were coded from the ground up. SQLite didn't exist before SQLite. If you examine the people + their process behind these repos:
- Fabrice Bellard, a generational programmer, has multiple of his repos represented in ProgramBench (tinycc, quickjs, ffmpeg). if you look at the dev history for these projects, it's him as a single contributor, writing extremely elegant + performant code with little to no dependencies, that achieves insane performance. (e.g. quickjs, a JS engine, is written in a few C files with literally 0 dependencies).
- David Peter (Sharkdp on Github, a member of @astral_sh, who wrote bat/fd/hexyl/pastel, used in ProgramBench) is another open source god who I really think exemplifies how excellent, widely used software is often not stitched together cuts of existing pieces of the internet, but more just a product of incredible ingenuity.

So to summarize point 2, my take is that incredible open source software that has lifted entire industries (e.g. ffmpeg to Youtube is https://xkcd.com/2347/), is really a product of insanely talented 100x developers; the internet is optional, and often not necessary for the top 1% of folks like this.

So back to the main point - the goal w/ ProgramBench is to reliably, rigorously investigate a coding agent's ability to build something from nothing. When a model inevitably starts getting non-0% resolve rate, our formulation allows us to say, with absolute certainty, that models have accomplished something superhuman. Unfortunately, at scale, internet access would taint, not reinforce the implications we want ProgramBench to make.

Some food for thought: enabling limited internet access for any single task is feasible a bit of hand tuning. The bigger question is ensure internet w/ 0 chance of cheating at scale.

That said, I'm looking forward to see where people run with this. The general premise of rearchitecting a program from scratch is a scalable, widely applicable formulation, and I'm excited about how we can expand on new tasks / inference settings (just like SWE-bench => Multimodal, Multilingual, Live, Pro, Rebench and many others :D)

posts.creator: kunchenguid
posts.text:
ProgramBench is interesting - it asks models to recreate real programs (ffmpeg, SQLite, ripgrep) from scratch with no internet

... but I hope no one actually optimizes for this benchmark

just think what's the solution that'll get 100% on this bench? it's a deterministic program that has the current source code of ffmepg, SQLite, ripgrep etc baked in, and just spit them out when asked

it can accidentally incentivize models that are good at memorizing answers from training data into its weights. these models tend to be unnecessarily big and expensive. it also penalizes models that are resourceful and great at leveraging the Internet

i want models that are cheap, fast and prefers using latest information from the Internet, and this benchmark rewards the opposite

quote.text:
How much of SQLite, FFmpeg, PHP compiler can LMs code from scratch? Given just an executable and no starter code or internet access.

Introducing ProgramBench: 200 rigorous, whole-repo generation tasks where models design, build, and ship a working program end to end. 🧵

posts.text:
this is why AI is both amazing and a slop machine at the same time

the differentiating factor is not AI. it's the human steering it

AI does two things
- it raises the floor of human capability. anyone can now code, design, and create stuff
- it amplifies the human

when the human's competence and capability at steering AI is above a threshold, they can almost infinitely scale up their capability - this is scarily powerful

when the human has poor judgment and taste, AI also amplifies it, creating slop that's even worse than what they'd do without AI

in the middle, AI helps a little but nothing transformative

these 3 buckets explain largely what we're seeing today
